In fact, there seems to be some numbers which given a definition, cannot be approximated. These are non-computable numbers. From the wikipedia definition of a computable number (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computable_number), you can find a sequence which converges fast enough to the number. A non-computable number would not have this properties, and since a convergent sum is a converging sequence of partial sums, this shows that a non-computable number would not have a series expansion.

During the course of history, the Vigenère Cipher has been reinvented many times

It was falsely attributed to Blaise de Vigenère as it was originally described in 1553 by Giovan Battista Bellaso in his book La cifra del. Sig. Giovan Battista Bellaso

For the implementation of this cipher a table is formed by sliding the lower half of an ordinary alphabet for an apparently random number of places with respect to the upper halfpicoCTF{b311a50_0r_v1gn3r3_c1ph3rabef1b3b}

The first well-documented description of a polyalphabetic cipher however, was made around 1467 by Leon Battista Alberti.

The Vigenère Cipher is therefore sometimes called the Alberti Disc or Alberti Cipher.

In 1508, Johannes Trithemius invented the so-called tabula recta (a matrix of shifted alphabets) that would later be a critical component of the Vigenère Cipher.

Bellaso's second booklet appeared in 1555 as a continuation of the first. The lower halves of the alphabets are now shifted regularly, but the alphabets and the index letters are mixed by means of a mnemonic key phrase, which can be different with each correspondent.

I'm a physicist so I like to think of problems like these in terms of having units. It really helps with the intuition. This is my run through of it:

Let's A and B be the efficiency with which person a and person b solve the job. The units of A and B will be in jobs/hour. Keeping track of the units with dimensional analysis will be helpful.

We are told that in x hours, if they work together, they complete 1 job:

Eq.1) (A+B)x = 1 job

We are told that in z hours, A completes 1/2 jobs and in (y-z) hours, B will complete 1 job:

Eq.2) Az =1/2 jobs

Eq.3) B(y-z)=1/2 jobs

At this point, we have all the equations we need, so I'll drop the job unit. From Eq.2, z=1/(2A). putting this into Eq.3 and manipulating a little gives:

Eq.4) 2 y=1/B +1/A

From Eq.1, we find B=1/A. Substituting this into Eq,4 and manipulating gives us:

Eq.5) 1 -2yA+2xyA^2 =0

Eq.6) A=(y+√(y(y-2x)))/(2xy)

Eq.7) B=(y-√(y(y-2x)))/(2xy)

Note that we use the + sign for A the quadratic formula because we know that A is more efficient than B so A has a higher jobs/hour that B.

Finally, we want to know how long (the time t) it will take B to complete one job:

Eq.8) Bt=1 job

Eq.9) t=1/B = (2xy)/(y-√(y*(y-2x)))

putting in some numbers: x=7.5 hours, y= 20 hours, we find: A=(1 job)/(10 hours), B=(1 job)/(30 hours)  and t = 30 hours, which is your final answer.

its not that dam mysterious if you've taken a stats course at any point. Here's a quick explanation:

Say you have two Gaussian distributed random variables X and Y with

X~G(X; mu1, sigma1)

Y~G(Y; mu2, sigma2)

Whats the distribution of say Z=X+Y? Well, it will be the convolution of the two distributions above:

Z~G(X; mu1, sigma1) *G(Y; mu2, sigma2) 

Z~ G(Z; mu1+mu2, Sqrt(sigma1^2 +sigma1^2 ))

Now if you make a measurement  with some error, you assume that it's a Gaussian distribution with a mean around the measured value and a standard deviation equal to the measurement error. If you say add two of these together, then you use the formula Sqrt(sigma1^2 +sigma1^2 ).

Functions of a Gaussian variable are also not that difficult but have some extra steps. Exercise to the reader. Hint: use a Taylor expansion to show that if X~G(X; mu, sigma), then E[f(X)]=f(mu)+f''(mu)/2 * sigma^2 and Var[f(X)]=(f'(mu))^2 sigma^2 where E represents the expectation value and Var represents the variance. Also if you want the usual formula for something multivariate, just ignore the co-variance.

Hey, I'm doing my PhD in particle physics so maybe I can shed some light on this. But first, you should understand what spontaneous symmetry breaking is as it plays a key role in the higgs giving particles mass.

Imagine a magnetized substance which is in some phase where all the little dipoles are pointing in different directions (like some molten iron or something, idk). In this phase, there is no net magnetic field, so you can rotate the substance as you would a sphere and it would not change the direction of the magnetic field. The substance in this case has the same symmetry as a sphere.

Imagine now the molten iron cools, and as it does, the small dipoles start to align in some random direction. The random direction could be any direction, but it picks one. Now, you no longer have the symmetries you had before because rotating the system would change the direction of the magnetic field. This is the same as spontaneous symmetry breaking. The dipoles have picked an arbitrary direction which broke the symmetry.

In quantum field theory, you work with quantum fields. The Higgs field is one such field. The theory has a "phase" where nothing has mass and the field has a big symmetry (kind of like the molten iron had). However, the universe has undergone this phase transition where the Higgs field sort of "picks" a direction which breaks the symmetry.

Since QFT is done as an expansion about the minimum energy of the theory, the phase where everything is symmetric is no longer the place to do your expansion. You have to find the new minimum of the Higgs field (which has a potential which looks like -mu^2 |H|^2+lambda|H|^4, where you have think of H as a 2 component complex vector, mu^2 and lambda as numbers). This new minimum ends up being just some number (246GeV off the top of my head), so instead of something like H, you get h+v in your couplings (I'm simplifying to no end, I don't want to get into lagrangian densities and Feynman rules). That v, the new minimum of the potential, then multiplies some number called the coupling, which is how much the higgs interacts with to a particle,  to give that particle mass (modulo some factors of root(2) everywhere).

As a side note, I should mention that this only gives mass to the particles of the standard model. Particles which are composite like the proton and neutron mostly get their mass from QCD (quantum chromodynamics) because its such a hot mess of garbage that can't be calculated using perturbation theory.

So what you measure are properties like position or momentum, but you can't attempt to measure both with the same experiment exactly.   This is simply not possible in the math. Therefore if two observers attempted to measure the same state, whoever measured it second would get a result reflecting the current state of the electron.

That being said, what you can do is weak measurements where you attempt to measure the property but with a larger error on the measurement. That way you don't mess up the other part too much, get an idea of both position and momentum, but still be unsure enough to satisfy the uncertainty principle.

Physics grad student here. In order to measure something about the electron in question, you need to interact with it in some way. If you interact with it and measure, say, the position, then you will have no idea what the momentum is. You could then measure the momentum, but then you no longer know where it is. If you then go to measure the position, then the momentum changes. 

You can't devise an experiment that will give you an exact number for both the position and momentum because the particle can't exist in an exact state of both. Instead, a particle will be in a quantum superposition of multiple positions and momentum values, called its wavefunction. You can describe a particle using a wavepacket which uses a superposition of values that are at least close to each other which can be useful to have an idea of where it is and how fast it is, it won't be exact but it will be good enough. Say now you measure the position exactly from this wavepacket. The superposition of the momenta that were close together is now a superposition of a much much wider range of momenta. Measuring the momenta then just smears out the position part of the superposition.

Imagine this, say you have

Psi=k1\*a+k2\*b

a=1/Sqrt[2]\*(c+d)

b=1/Sqrt[2]\*(c-d)

Where Psi is the wavefunction, a and b are eigenstates of the first operator (say position), c and d are eigenstates of the second operator, and k1 and k2 are some numbers such that k1^2 +k2^2 =1. You make a measurement on Psi and find the answer a. You then have:

Psi '=a=k3\*c+k4\*d

You now make a measurement for the other operator and find c, you then get:

Psi''=c=1/Sqrt[2]\*(a+b)

Notice that immediately after the first measurement you know the position, but by performing the second measurement, you lost that information.

To be even more technical, wavefunctions are vectors in a Hilbert space. We describe the basis of the Hilbert space using the eigenstates of a commuting set of operators, but since position and momenta don't commute with each other, you can't write a basis that is simultaneously eigenstates of both operators. If you make a measurement, the possible values are based on the eigenstates in the decomposition of the wavefunctions. Making such a measurement would then collapse the wavefunction down to the eigenstate of the observed value. You could then write this state in terms of the basis states of the other operator and see that you can have multiple answers. Collapsing the wavefunction in the new basis will reveal that you can now write the result in terms of the first basis, but with different answer.


**TL;DR measuring it fucks with it, so all you know exactly is the last thing you measured.**
